title: Reliability, safety and failure analysis
note: Reliability is the probability that a system performs its function for a stated time under stated conditions. Series systems are only as reliable as the product of their parts; redundancy in parallel raises reliability. FMEA works bottom-up through each way a part can fail. Famous failures mostly trace to untested assumptions, unchecked changes, and ignored warnings.

read.title: Lessons written in failure
text: Engineering learns hardest from its failures. In 1940 the new Tacoma Narrows Bridge twisted itself apart in a 40 mph wind. Its slender deck of shallow plate girders was too flexible, and wind drove a self-excited twisting called flutter. Bridge decks have been tested for aerodynamic stability ever since.

During World War II, cracks raced through the welded hulls of Liberty ships, and a few broke in two. Constance Tipper showed that the steel turned brittle in cold water. Cracks started at square hatch corners, and the continuous welded hull had no seams to stop them. Engineers now specify steels tough at low temperature and avoid sharp corners.

In 1981 two walkways fell in the Kansas City Hyatt Regency, killing 114 people. A change from one continuous rod to two offset rods doubled the load on a connection, and the change was approved without being checked by calculation.
In January 1986, cold weather stiffened the O-rings sealing Space Shuttle Challenger's booster joints. Engineers had warned against launching in the cold, but their warning was overruled.
The physics in each case was known. The failures came from untested assumptions, unchecked changes, and ignored warnings, which is why tools such as FMEA and design reviews exist.

q.q: What made the Hyatt Regency connection fail?
o: A rod change that doubled its load

q.q: According to the reading, what did Constance Tipper find?
o: The steel became brittle in cold water

q.q: What common thread links these failures?
o: Untested assumptions, unchecked changes, and ignored warnings
